sentences.text: Spinosaurus mirabilis possessed a long, low snout whose dorsal and ventral edges ran nearly parallel, a scimitar-shaped crest along the skull midline, and a prominent sail formed by extremely elongated neural spines on its back.
A gap (diastema) in the upper jaw allowed three large teeth from the lower jaw to fit when the mouth closed.

The premaxilla at the front of the snout was slightly more arched and rose above the rest of the snout, while the front part of the lower jaw broadened into a roughly square shape, differing from the rounder form seen in S. aegyptiacus.
Compared with its close relative, the rear maxillary teeth were spaced more widely, and the snout was proportionally lower.
Evidence from specimen MNBH JEN4 hints that the hind limbs may have been relatively longer than those of S. aegyptiacus.
Only juvenile material has been recovered, leaving the adult dimensions uncertain.
The type locality lies within the Farak Formation of Niger.
The holotype, catalogued as MNBH JEN1, consists of fragments of the right premaxilla, both maxillae, a nasal crest, part of the right dentary, and five maxillary teeth.
Additional material (MNBH JEN2) includes a portion of the left maxilla, another nasal crest fragment, pieces of neck and back vertebrae, and parts of the left ischium and femur.
The most diagnostic fossils were recovered at the Jenguebi site during field seasons in 2019 and 2022 under Paul Sereno’s direction.
Sereno and colleagues reported seven incomplete specimens from Jenguebi and Iguidi in 2026, and later counts raise the total to fourteen known specimens.
Specimens from Jenguebi are stored at the University Abdou Moumouni, while those from Iguidi are temporarily loaned to Sereno’s laboratory at the University of Chicago.
Initially the holotype material from the 2019 campaign was misidentified as a dentary of a carcharodontosaurid theropod, according to Daniel Vidal.
The interior fluvial deposits that yielded S. mirabilis suggest it inhabited riverine and freshwater settings rather than coastal marine environments.
Spinosaurus mirabilis is regarded as a close relative of the sail-backed, fish-eating Spinosaurus aegyptiacus.
Specimen IGU11, once assigned to Carcharodontosaurus iguidensis and later to Sigilmassasaurus brevicollis, has been reinterpreted in 2026 as possibly belonging to S. mirabilis.
Spinosaurus mirabilis lived during the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.

Its occurrence in interior river deposits aligns with the final evolutionary phase of spinosaurines, during which they reached maximal size as shallow-water ambush specialists in northern Africa and South America.
Researchers continue to discuss whether S. mirabilis functioned as a semi-aquatic ambush predator or as a fully aquatic diver.
